opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think one of the most exciting things right now is how AI is starting to speed up the work of building AI itself. A lot of it isn't the dramatic "model rewrites its own weights" story people imagine. It's more practical, and in some ways more powerful.

Take data. For years I've talked about data-centric AI, the idea that systematically improving your data is often a better lever than tinkering with model architecture. Today we're seeing large models generate synthetic training data, clean and label datasets, find inconsistencies, and write evaluation sets. Work that used to take a team of people weeks can now be done much faster, which means smaller models and specialized models can get dramatically better at lower cost.

Then there's the agentic side. AI coding assistants are already making engineers, including AI researchers, much more productive. When you can prototype an idea in an afternoon instead of a week, you run many more experiments, and the pace of innovation goes up. I think we're underestimating how much that rapid iteration loop compounds over time.

I'd add one note of grounding. Humans are still very much in the loop: deciding what problems matter, judging whether a result is meaningful, and making sure systems are built responsibly. I see AI helping build AI less as a runaway process and more as a powerful tool that lets researchers and builders move faster. And because these tools keep getting cheaper and more accessible, a lot more people around the world will be able to take part in building the next generation of AI applications. That's the part I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response mentions synthetic training data and faster AI development, but does not describe an older model generating puzzles through prolonged reasoning for a successor to solve with less reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the thing that excites me most is actually a little different from what people usually mean when they talk about recursive self-improvement. The dramatic version, where a model goes off and designs its successor and we all step back, I'm frankly skeptical of that, at least in the near term. What I'm seeing, and what I find genuinely exciting, is much more mundane and much more real.

If you look at what it takes to build a frontier model today, a huge fraction of the work isn't the big architectural insight. It's data. It's cleaning data, labeling data, filtering web crawls, generating synthetic examples for the long tail of cases where you just don't have enough real-world coverage. It's writing evals. It's debugging why the loss curve did something weird at step forty thousand. And a lot of that work is exactly the kind of thing that current models are already quite good at.

So when I talk to teams, the pattern I see over and over is that models are being used to curate training data for the next model, to grade outputs, to act as judges, to generate the preference data for alignment. Hiring thousands of human annotators used to be a bottleneck, and now a lot of that can be done with a model in the loop, with humans supervising and spot-checking rather than doing every example. That compresses the iteration cycle dramatically. And in machine learning, speed of iteration is almost everything. If you can run twice as many experiments in the same amount of time, you learn twice as fast.

The other piece I find exciting is on the coding side. I've been writing code for a long time, and the way I write code has changed completely in the last couple of years. The researchers building these models are now using AI coding assistants to write their training infrastructure, their data pipelines, their evaluation harnesses. So even if the model isn't inventing the next breakthrough, it's making the humans who do that work maybe two or three times more productive. That's a very real feedback loop, just a less cinematic one.

Now, I do want to add a note of caution, because I think it matters. When you train on model-generated data, you have to be really careful about distribution collapse, about the model just amplifying its own biases and blind spots. The teams that do this well are very disciplined about keeping humans and real-world data in the loop as a grounding signal. So I don't think of this as "AI builds AI." I think of it as AI dramatically lowering the cost of the tedious parts of research, which frees up smart people to spend their time on the hard conceptual problems. And that, to me, is the exciting part. It democratizes who can build these systems. A small team today can do what took a hundred people a few years ago, and I think that's going to lead to a lot more experimentation and a lot more surprising ideas coming from places we don't expect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models helping with data curation, evaluation, and coding, but does not describe training a successor on puzzles generated through prolonged reasoning so it can solve them with less reasoning.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the potential to make the research process much faster. When you’re developing a model, you have an idea, you write code, you run an experiment, and then you try to understand why it worked or didn’t work. AI can help with more of that cycle—not just writing the code, but examining the results and suggesting what to try next.

I think the interesting question is: how much of that loop can we automate reliably? Generating a lot of ideas is useful, but you still need good experiments and a way to distinguish a real improvement from noise. If we can get that right, a small team could explore many more directions than it could before. That’s a very exciting prospect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automating AI research and experiments, but does not describe an older model generating puzzles through prolonged reasoning or training a successor to solve them with less reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing that excites me is how much faster we can make the experimentation loop. Building AI involves a lot of work: writing code, preparing data, running experiments, and trying to understand why something didn’t work. AI can help with all of those steps.

But the part I find especially interesting is using these tools to explore more ideas. A researcher might have ten hypotheses and only enough time to test two. If AI helps us test more of them, we have a better chance of discovering something useful.

The challenge is making sure we can evaluate the results. Generating a plausible idea or a piece of code is different from demonstrating that it improves a model. So I’m excited about systems that propose an experiment, run it, check the evidence, and help a human decide what to try next. That could make research much more productive and allow smaller teams to contribute as well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI speeding up research experiments, but does not describe generating puzzles through prolonged reasoning by an older model or training a successor to solve them with less reasoning.
